quickStart: For an immediate threat to life or safety, call Triple Zero (000). From a mobile, 112 may connect to emergency services; use 106 text emergency service if you have a speech or hearing impairment.
For urgent health advice when it is not a life-threatening emergency, call healthdirect on 1800 022 222.
For poison advice, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
Locate and securely extract the Onter ZIP. Review emergency contacts, health details, legal document locations, insurance, banks, super, and essential liabilities first.
If someone has died, identify the authorised representative and contact each provider using its official bereavement process. Do not access accounts or use credentials without authority.
Keep the export encrypted and do not store passwords, PINs, authentication codes, myGov/myID credentials, or recovery keys in it.

firstActions: Check identifiers against official records
Protect TFN details and share them only when required
Keep the current address and contacts updated

Emergency contact details.description: Trusted people and their possible roles; this list does not itself create decision-making or account authority.
firstActions: Confirm each person knows they are listed
Verify phone and email details
Locate separate formal appointment documents when legal authority is needed

Health and Care Information.description: Optional care information and locations of formal directives.
firstActions: Call 000 for life-threatening emergencies
Tell clinicians about known allergies and current medicines
Locate any valid advance care directive and confirm state or territory requirements

Insurance details.description: Private, employer, home, and other policies; some life and disability cover may be held through superannuation.
firstActions: Find current policy schedules and claims contacts
Check cover and beneficiary or nomination details with the provider
Ask about time limits and required evidence

firstActions: Confirm account holders and authorities with the bank
Use the provider's bereavement process
Keep statements in secure storage

firstActions: Confirm ownership and current valuations with providers

legalNotes: This guide is general information, not legal, tax, insurance, or financial advice.
Wills, powers of attorney, guardianship, and advance-care laws and document names vary by Australian state and territory.
Superannuation may be administered under fund rules and a death-benefit nomination; do not assume super automatically forms part of the estate or follows the will.
The ATO states Australia has no inheritance tax, but final personal and estate tax returns, capital gains tax, and super tax may still apply. Check current ATO guidance.
Official: Triple Zero emergency information: https://www.triplezero.gov.au/
Official: ATO checklist after a death: https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/deceased-estates/checklist-what-to-do-when-someone-dies

fileStructure: The export ZIP may contain a spreadsheet, PDFs, and this access guide.
Treat every file as sensitive; it may include identity, health, financial, and legal references.
dataAccess: Extract to a private, encrypted location and keep an untouched backup.
Share only with trusted authorised people; a family relationship alone does not grant legal access.
Store credentials in a reputable password manager with an emergency-access feature, not in this export.
securityTips: Never put passwords, PINs, TFN portal credentials, authentication codes, or recovery keys in the export.
Use encrypted storage and secure channels for sensitive documents.
Review after major life events and at least annually; remove outdated copies securely.

recoveryRoadmap.description: A general checklist after a death. Confirm the relevant state or territory process and your authority before acting.

meta.title: Family Recovery Roadmap - Australia
meta.reviewedBy: Federal sources reviewed; state and territory legal review remains necessary

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This checklist is intended to make the first practical steps clearer.
intro.howToUse: Confirm who is authorised to act, secure records, contact relevant providers, and obtain local legal or tax advice where needed.

startHere: Follow the state or territory death-registration process and ask which documents are required.
Locate the will and identify the executor or other authorised representative.
Contact Services Australia, the ATO, banks, insurers, employers, and super funds through official bereavement processes.
List assets, debts, regular bills, and claims; confirm responsibility before changing payments or distributing property.
Keep a log of calls, documents supplied, and provider decisions. Never access an account without authority.
legalFramework: State and territory probate, succession, powers-of-attorney, and guardianship rules.
ATO rules for the final tax return and any deceased-estate tax returns.
Super fund governing rules and death-benefit nominations; super may be treated differently from estate assets.
Current Services Australia, insurance, creditor, and provider claim requirements.

phases.title: Secure records and authority
phases.focus: Register the death as directed, identify the authorised representative, and protect records.

keyActions.action: Follow local registration instructions and obtain the record or certificate required by each organisation.
keyActions.why: State and territory registration and certificate processes vary.

keyActions.action: Find the will, identify the executor, and get legal advice if no will or a dispute exists.
keyActions.why: Authority to deal with the estate must be established before assets are administered.

mustHaveDocuments: Bank, super, insurance, property, and debt references
criticalMistakes: Assuming next of kin can operate accounts
Assuming one state's legal forms apply throughout Australia
Putting passwords or myGov codes in an exported record

phases.title: Notify and identify claims
phases.focus: Notify public bodies and private providers, and preserve a reliable asset and liability list.

keyActions.action: Notify the ATO and Services Australia using their current bereavement processes.
keyActions.why: Government records, payments, and tax correspondence may need to be updated.

keyActions.action: Contact each bank, insurer, employer, and super fund separately; ask about forms, nominations, benefits, and payment arrangements.
keyActions.why: Government notification does not close every private account or submit every claim.

mustHaveDocuments: List of recurring bills and debts
criticalMistakes: Paying debts before confirming legal responsibility

phases.title: Administer and finalise
phases.focus: Complete required tax and legal steps before final distribution.

keyActions.action: Confirm whether probate or letters of administration are needed under the relevant state or territory process.
keyActions.why: Requirements depend on the estate, assets, and institutions holding them.

keyActions.action: Check the final individual tax return and any estate tax returns with the ATO or a registered tax agent.
keyActions.why: Tax affairs may continue after death and should be addressed before final distribution.

mustHaveDocuments: Grant or administration documents if required
criticalMistakes: Distributing assets before confirming tax and creditor obligations
Assuming no tax filings are needed

phases.title: Review family arrangements
phases.focus: Review the surviving household's estate, super, insurance, and secure information arrangements.

keyActions.action: Review wills, powers of attorney, super nominations, insurance beneficiaries, and emergency contacts with relevant professionals.
keyActions.why: Major life changes can make existing appointments or nominations unsuitable.
keyActions.legalRef: State or territory legislation and fund rules

keyActions.action: Keep a current asset and digital-account index; store credentials only in a suitable password manager.
keyActions.why: A secure index can help authorised people find records without exposing secrets.

criticalMistakes: Sharing passwords in the family record

emergency.number: 000; 112 from mobile; 106 text emergency service for speech/hearing impairment

taxAfterDeath.note: The ATO may require a final individual return and deceased-estate returns. Confirm current requirements before distributing assets.

super.note: Contact each super fund about death benefits, fund rules, nominations, and tax treatment.

glossary.definition: An executor or administrator with authority recognised for dealing with a deceased estate.
A benefit paid under superannuation law and fund rules; the recipient and tax treatment depend on the circumstances and nomination.
A court grant recognising an executor's authority to administer an estate; when required varies by state or territory and institution.
